chapter_summary:
Disaster Recovery (DR) is about preparing for and recovering from major disruptions that could affect an entire AWS Region or a significant portion of your infrastructure. Unlike high availability, which focuses on component failures within a single operational environment, DR addresses widespread, catastrophic events. Choosing the right DR strategy is a critical decision that balances your business's tolerance for downtime and data loss (RTO and RPO) against the cost and complexity of implementation. AWS offers a spectrum of strategies, each with different RTO/RPO characteristics and cost profiles.

The simplest and often most cost-effective DR strategy is **Backup and Restore**. This approach involves regularly backing up your data (e.g., EBS snapshots, RDS automated backups, S3 objects) and storing it in a separate, often remote, location (e.g., another AWS Region). In the event of a disaster, you would restore your data from these backups to a newly provisioned infrastructure in the recovery Region. This strategy typically has the highest RTO (hours to days) and RPO (minutes to hours, depending on backup frequency) because it involves provisioning infrastructure from scratch and restoring large datasets. It's suitable for non-critical applications or data that can tolerate significant downtime and some data loss. The cost is relatively low, primarily for storage of backups.

Moving up the scale in terms of RTO/RPO and cost, we have the **Pilot Light** strategy. This strategy involves keeping a minimal, "pilot light" set of core infrastructure components running in the recovery Region. This might include a small database instance with replicated data, or a few EC2 instances with the application code pre-installed but not actively serving traffic. The idea is that the "pilot light" is always on and ready to quickly scale up. In a disaster, you would provision additional resources (e.g., scale up EC2 instances, launch new application servers from AMIs) and direct traffic to the recovery Region. Pilot Light offers lower RTO (tens of minutes to hours) and RPO (minutes to hours, depending on data replication) than Backup and Restore because some infrastructure is already in place and data is continuously replicated. The cost is moderate, as you're paying for some active resources in the DR Region.

The **Warm Standby** strategy takes Pilot Light a step further. With Warm Standby, you maintain a scaled-down but fully functional version of your application in the recovery Region. This means you have active EC2 instances, databases, and other services running, but perhaps at a reduced capacity or only handling non-critical traffic. The data is continuously replicated, and the application is ready to take over with minimal effort. In a disaster, you would simply scale up the existing resources in the recovery Region and redirect traffic. Warm Standby provides even lower RTO (minutes to tens of minutes) and RPO (seconds to minutes) than Pilot Light because the application stack is largely operational. The cost is higher than Pilot Light, as you are running more active resources in the DR Region, but still less than a full active-active setup.

Finally, the most robust and expensive strategy is **Multi-Site Active/Active** (sometimes called Hot Standby). In this approach, your application is fully deployed and actively serving traffic in multiple AWS Regions simultaneously. Users are typically routed to the nearest active Region using services like Amazon Route 53. Data replication is continuous and often synchronous or near-synchronous between Regions. In the event of a regional disaster, traffic is immediately routed away from the affected Region to the healthy Region(s) with virtually no downtime or data loss. This strategy offers the lowest RTO (seconds to minutes) and RPO (near zero) but comes with the highest cost and operational complexity, as you are essentially running your entire application stack in duplicate or triplicate. It's reserved for mission-critical applications where even minutes of downtime or seconds of data loss are unacceptable.

When choosing a strategy, a common mistake is to default to the most expensive option (Multi-Site Active/Active) without a clear business justification. Always start by defining your RTO and RPO requirements with business stakeholders. If your business can tolerate an RTO of 4 hours and an RPO of 1 hour, a Backup and Restore or Pilot Light strategy might be sufficient and far more cost-effective than Warm Standby or Active/Active. Another pitfall is underestimating the complexity of data replication, especially for databases. Ensuring data consistency across regions for a Multi-Site Active/Active setup can be challenging and requires careful design. Safety note: regardless of the strategy chosen, regular testing of your DR plan is non-negotiable. An untested DR plan is a liability, not an asset. You need to validate that your RTO and RPO targets are actually achievable in a real-world scenario.

screens.title: Disaster Recovery Strategies on AWS
screens.subtitle: Choose an approach that balances recovery time, data loss tolerance, and cost

narration.text: In this lesson you will build a clear mental model for four AWS disaster recovery strategies and why each exists. We will compare Backup and Restore, Pilot Light, Warm Standby, and Multi-Site Active/Active by their recovery time objective and recovery point objective, and by the cost and operational effort they demand. You will learn how to match a business requirement—say, a database that must recover within 30 minutes with only five minutes of data loss—to a realistic strategy, and you will see common traps teams fall into, like choosing the most expensive option without justification. A practical activity at the end will ask you to design a DR approach for a three-tier application and map services to meet RTO and RPO goals. By the end of the module you will be able to explain trade-offs to stakeholders, create a testable DR plan, and pick the most cost-effective approach for each workload. Think of this as a decision toolkit: requirements in, recommended strategy out.

keyIdea.title: Core Insight
keyIdea.text: DR is a choice between downtime/data-loss tolerance and ongoing cost/complexity. Match RTO/RPO to strategy and validate with tests.

screens.title: RTO and RPO — The Foundations of DR
screens.subtitle: Define what recovery time and recovery point mean for your business

narration.text: RTO and RPO are the foundational metrics that drive every disaster recovery choice. Recovery Time Objective, or RTO, is the maximum acceptable time the system can be unavailable after an incident. Recovery Point Objective, or RPO, is the maximum acceptable age of the data when recovery completes—effectively, how much data loss you can tolerate. Together they form the business inputs that determine how much you must invest in infrastructure and operational readiness. For example, if a payments database requires an RTO of 30 minutes and an RPO of 5 minutes, synchronous or near-synchronous replication and a warm standby or active-active approach might be required. A common misconception is to treat RTO and RPO as purely technical targets; they are business decisions. Another trap is to assume low RPO implies low RTO automatically—while related, achieving both often increases cost and complexity. Practical takeaway: always ask the stakeholder two questions: how long can users be down, and how much data loss is acceptable? Those answers immediately narrow the viable DR strategies. To check understanding, state the RTO and RPO for a non-critical reporting job and see which low-cost option fits.

keyIdea.title: Definition
keyIdea.text: RTO is acceptable downtime; RPO is acceptable data loss. Both drive strategy choice.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › RTO & RPO

RTO and RPO — The Foundations of DR

Clear definitions let you compare strategies objectively.

Definitions
Recovery Time Objective (RTO)
Maximum acceptable downtime after a failure. Measured in seconds, minutes, or hours.
Recovery Point Objective (RPO)
Maximum acceptable data loss, expressed as the age of the most recent recoverable data.
Why it matters
These two numbers determine how much infrastructure and replication you need and help prioritize DR spend.
Key Takeaway

Ask stakeholders for specific RTO and RPO values before proposing a DR strategy; these narrow choices quickly.

Concrete example & common misconception
Example
A database with RTO 30 minutes and RPO 5 minutes pushes you toward continuous replication and a warm standby or active-active model to meet both targets.
Misconception
Low RPO does not guarantee low RTO. You can have frequent backups (low RPO) but still take hours to provision infrastructure (high RTO).
Check your understanding
Pick a non-critical analytics job and propose acceptable RTO/RPO. If they are hours and a day, Backup and Restore is likely sufficient.

screens.title: Backup and Restore
screens.subtitle: Lowest cost; highest recovery time — when to use it

narration.text: Backup and Restore is the simplest AWS disaster recovery approach and often the most cost-effective. It relies on regular snapshots and object backups stored in a separate region or account. In a disaster you provision new infrastructure in the recovery region and restore data from those backups. Typical recovery steps are: ensure backups exist, provision necessary VPCs and compute, restore storage or databases from snapshots, reconfigure endpoints, and resume traffic. This leads to higher RTO — from hours to days — and RPO depends on backup frequency. Use this strategy for non-critical workloads or data that can tolerate extended downtime. A common mistake is to assume backups alone equal recoverability; if infrastructure provisioning is not automated, restore times balloon. Automate provisioning with templates or scripts to reduce RTO, and test restores regularly. Example: daily EBS snapshots and S3 object versioning for internal reporting can be enough since the business accepts a day of data loss. Final takeaway: Backup and Restore minimizes cost but requires documented and tested restore runbooks to be reliable. Backup and Restore means low cost, high rto — suitable when downtime and data loss tolerance are large and restores are tested.. In practical terms, lowest cost; highest recovery time — when to use it. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Backup & Restore
keyIdea.text: Low cost, high RTO — suitable when downtime and data loss tolerance are large and restores are tested.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Backup & Restore

Backup and Restore

Store backups in a separate location and restore infrastructure when needed.

Process Steps
1.
Schedule and store backups (EBS, RDS snapshots, S3 versioning).
2.
Keep backups in a separate region or account.
3.
Provision recovery infrastructure (VPC, subnets, compute) when needed.
4.
Restore data, reconfigure endpoints, and bring services online.
Key Takeaway

Use when low cost is priority and long RTOs are acceptable. Automate provisioning to shorten recovery time.

Example, pitfall, and checklist
Example
Internal reporting systems with daily snapshots and S3 backups that can tolerate hours or days of downtime.
Common pitfall
Backups without automated provisioning or tested restore procedures cause unexpectedly long RTOs.
Quick checklist
  • Backups exist and are cross-region.
  • Provisioning scripts or templates are available.
  • Restores are performed regularly as tests.

screens.title: Pilot Light
screens.subtitle: Keep the minimal critical core running to shorten recovery

narration.text: Pilot Light is a middle-ground strategy where a minimal set of core services are kept running in the recovery region. Think of it as a small, warm nucleus: the database replica and a few pre-configured application images are active, but they do not serve production traffic at scale. When a disaster occurs you expand those components by launching more servers, scaling auto-scaling groups, and attaching replicas to fuller capacity. Pilot Light improves RTO and RPO relative to Backup and Restore because data is continuously replicated and core elements already exist. The cost is moderate—you're paying for some persistent resources—but it is lower than running full stacks in multiple regions. A practical example is maintaining an RDS read replica in the recovery region and keeping AMIs with the application pre-baked. Common misconception: pilot light is not fully ready to serve heavy traffic instantly; plan automation to scale capacity quickly. Test by simulating scale-up so you measure true recovery time under load. The key idea: keep the minimal state that matters always on so recovery is mostly about scaling, not building. Pilot Light means minimal active core plus automated scale-up reduces recovery time and preserves recent data.. In practical terms, keep the minimal critical core running to shorten recovery. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Pilot Light
keyIdea.text: Minimal active core plus automated scale-up reduces recovery time and preserves recent data.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Pilot Light

Pilot Light

Run a minimal, replicated core in the DR region and scale up when needed.

Architecture snapshot
Always-on components
Lightweight DB replica, pre-baked application AMIs, and minimal networking in the recovery region.
Scale-up actions
Launch additional instances, scale ASGs, promote replicas, and update DNS or routing to cut over.
Typical RTO/RPO
RTO: tens of minutes to hours. RPO: minutes to hours depending on replication frequency.
Example, mistake, and test
Example
Keep an RDS read replica in the recovery region and AMIs for web servers that are kept patched and ready.
Common mistake
Assuming pilot light will handle peak load without rehearsed automation to scale and promote replicas.
Test
Simulate promotion of the replica and automated scaling to confirm the time to reach production capacity.

screens.title: Warm Standby
screens.subtitle: A scaled-down, serving copy ready to take over

narration.text: Warm Standby maintains a scaled-down but fully functional copy of your application in the recovery region. Unlike pilot light, which keeps only the minimal core active, warm standby runs the stack—compute, network, and a database replica—at reduced capacity. It accepts either low-level traffic or no traffic, but the components are already provisioned and warmed. In a disaster you scale up capacity and redirect traffic. Warm Standby gives lower RTO and RPO than pilot light because the services are already running and data replication is continuous. Costs are higher than pilot light due to more active resources, but far lower than a full active-active deployment. Use warm standby when you need short recovery windows but want to conserve some cost. A typical implementation uses a smaller instance class and fewer replicas in the DR region with automation to scale. Misconception to avoid: scaled-down does not mean untested—run realistic load tests to ensure the scaled configuration will behave predictably when scaled up. The practical benefit is faster recovery without full duplication. Warm Standby means a ready, scaled-down deployment that can be scaled to full capacity quickly with lower cost than active-active.. In practical terms, a scaled-down, serving copy ready to take over. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Warm Standby
keyIdea.text: A ready, scaled-down deployment that can be scaled to full capacity quickly with lower cost than active-active.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Warm Standby

Warm Standby

Keep a functional, scaled-down copy of systems ready to scale up when needed.

What it contains
Active components
Smaller ASGs, an active DB replica, networking, and monitoring—functional but at reduced capacity.
Failover action
Scale existing instances, increase ASG min sizes, promote replicas if needed, and switch routing to the DR region.
Expected RTO/RPO
RTO: minutes to tens of minutes. RPO: seconds to minutes under continuous replication.
Example, test, and caution
Example
A customer-facing application with high-value transactions that can tolerate short scaling time but not long outages.
Test
Perform scale-up rehearsals to ensure the standby configuration scales and latency stays acceptable under load.
Caution
Running active resources increases cost; balance instance sizing and automation to keep expected costs reasonable.

screens.title: Multi-Site Active/Active
screens.subtitle: Near-zero downtime and near-zero data loss at high cost

narration.text: Multi-Site Active/Active runs the application fully in multiple regions simultaneously, with traffic routed geographically or by health. It offers the lowest RTO and RPO—failover is immediate or automatic and data loss is near zero—because each region is already active. However, it requires careful design for cross-region data replication, session state management, and consistent configuration. Services like DNS routing, global caches, and synchronous or carefully orchestrated replication are required. For example, production traffic can be distributed using a routing policy that prefers the nearest healthy region, and databases must be designed to either tolerate eventual consistency or use actively replicated database services. The trade-offs are operational complexity and high cost because you run the full stack in multiple locations. Avoid defaulting to active-active simply because it seems safest; reserve it for mission-critical systems where even minutes of downtime are unacceptable. Practice scenario: a trading platform requiring near-zero RTO/RPO warrants active-active. Final takeaway: active-active delivers the fastest recovery but demands engineering effort to ensure global consistency and testability. Multi-Site Active/Active means full deployments in multiple regions for immediate failover and minimal data loss, with highest cost and complexity.. In practical terms, near-zero downtime and near-zero data loss at high cost. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Multi-Site Active/Active
keyIdea.text: Full deployments in multiple regions for immediate failover and minimal data loss, with highest cost and complexity.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Multi-Site Active/Active

Multi-Site Active/Active

Run full deployments in multiple regions for near-zero recovery impact.

Benefits & Requirements
Immediate failover
Traffic is routed to healthy regions with no infrastructure provisioning step required.
Replication needs
Continuous cross-region replication or globally consistent data stores are essential.
Operational demands
Configuration management, global testing, and runbooks must handle region failover scenarios.
Example & caution
Example
A globally distributed application, like a trading system, where even seconds of downtime are unacceptable.
Caution
Data consistency across regions can be challenging; design for conflict resolution or use services that support cross-region sync.
Cost note
Expect near-duplicate running costs because the full stack is active in each region.

screens.title: Mapping RTO/RPO to DR Strategies
screens.subtitle: How to pick the smallest effective strategy for a requirement

narration.text: Choosing a DR strategy starts with mapping explicit RTO and RPO requirements to options that meet them without unnecessary cost. A useful mental model is a spectrum: Backup and Restore covers high RTO and high RPO tolerance; Pilot Light lowers both by keeping a minimal core; Warm Standby further reduces RTO and RPO by running a scaled copy; Active/Active minimizes both but at high cost. Practically, gather stakeholder RTO and RPO targets per tier. For a database needing RPO of 5 minutes and RTO of 30 minutes, warm standby or active-active are candidates; pilot light may be insufficient unless replication frequency is extremely fast. For web servers with RTO of two hours and RPO of one hour, pilot light or Backup and Restore may be acceptable depending on automation. A common error is using a single strategy for all tiers—mix strategies per tier to optimize cost. Also beware optimistic assumptions about replication; measure replication lag. The decision process is: collect RTO/RPO, rank strategies that meet them, estimate cost/complexity, and validate with tests. This mapping, not ideological preference, should drive the choice.

keyIdea.title: Decision Rule
keyIdea.text: Match the minimum strategy that satisfies RTO/RPO for each tier; mix strategies to optimize cost.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Mapping RTO/RPO

Map RTO/RPO to DR Strategies

Use RTO and RPO per component to select an appropriate strategy and avoid one-size-fits-all errors.

Quick mapping guide
  • High RTO/RPO tolerance → Backup & Restore.
  • Moderate RTO/RPO → Pilot Light with replication.
  • Low RTO/RPO → Warm Standby with active replication.
  • Near-zero RTO/RPO → Multi-Site Active/Active.
Remember to treat each application tier independently and combine strategies where appropriate.
Concrete example
Tier 1: Database
RPO 5 minutes, RTO 30 minutes → Warm Standby or Active/Active (depending on cost tolerance).
Tier 2: Web/App
RPO 1 hour, RTO 2 hours → Pilot Light or Backup & Restore with automated provisioning.

screens.title: Cost vs Operational Complexity
screens.subtitle: Understand recurring and one-time costs and hidden operational work

narration.text: Cost and complexity vary widely across DR strategies. Backup and Restore has low recurring costs—mostly storage and occasional data-transfer—while labor and provisioning time create higher effective recovery costs when outages happen. Pilot Light increases ongoing cost because of minimal running resources, and automation effort rises to ensure smooth scale-up. Warm Standby raises costs further by running larger instance types and more services at baseline capacity. Multi-Site Active/Active has the highest ongoing cost because the full production stack runs in multiple regions; its operational complexity is also highest due to data consistency, monitoring, and global deployment management. Hidden costs include runbook maintenance, test exercises, and the engineering effort to design safe failovers. When you produce a cost estimate, include both monthly resource cost and expected operational effort: how many engineers and how many hours are needed to test and maintain the runbooks. A practical exercise is to tabulate monthly resource cost for each strategy and add an estimated monthly operational overhead—this makes trade-offs visible to stakeholders. Remember: cheaper up front may mean more costly outages later if tests are not performed and automation is incomplete.

keyIdea.title: Cost Trade-off
keyIdea.text: Include both recurring resource costs and operational overhead when comparing DR strategies.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Cost vs Complexity

Cost vs Operational Complexity

Look beyond resource bills to include engineering and testing effort in estimates.

Cost profile
Backup & Restore: storage costs; low baseline compute cost.
Pilot Light: small running footprint; moderate storage and compute costs.
Warm Standby: larger baseline compute; higher monthly cost.
Active/Active: near-duplicate costs across regions; highest monthly bill.
Operational overhead
Maintain runbooks and test plans; schedule and perform failover rehearsals.
Monitor replication lag and automated scaling behavior.
Manage configuration drift across regions and enforce parity where necessary.

screens.title: Data Replication and Consistency
screens.subtitle: Why replication design affects RPO and operational risk

narration.text: Data replication is central to reducing RPO, but it introduces complexity that affects correctness and recoverability. Replication can be asynchronous, near-synchronous, or synchronous. Asynchronous replication is simpler and cheaper but can lead to data loss during failover if the most recent writes haven't arrived in the DR region. Synchronous replication minimizes data loss because writes complete only when acknowledged by replicas, but it increases latency and can be costly or impractical across long-distance links. For distributed databases, eventual consistency is another model that requires application-level conflict handling. A common pitfall is underestimating replication lag and treating replication as an instantaneous guarantee. Always measure replication lag under load and include it in your RPO calculations. For relational databases, managed read replicas or cross-region read replicas can help, but promoting replicas typically requires careful steps to ensure transactional integrity. The practical rule: design replication to meet the declared RPO and document the expected worst-case lag, then test it with realistic traffic patterns to confirm the claim. In practical terms, why replication design affects rpo and operational risk. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Replication
keyIdea.text: Replication mode determines actual RPO. Measure lag and design for consistency requirements.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Replication & Consistency

Data Replication and Consistency

Replication choices directly influence achievable RPO and system behavior under failover.

Replication modes
Asynchronous: cheaper, possible data loss during failover.
Near-synchronous: lower lag, moderate cost.
Synchronous: minimal data loss, higher latency and cost.
Practical guidance
Measure replication lag under production load and include worst-case lag in your RPO statement.
Design conflict resolution or choose a database that supports the required cross-region semantics.
Don't assume managed read replicas are drop-in for failover; promotion steps and consistency guarantees vary.

screens.title: Testing and Validating Your DR Plan
screens.subtitle: Turn assumptions into measured evidence

narration.text: A DR plan is only as good as its tests. Regular validation confirms that documented RTO and RPO targets are achievable. Tests should be scheduled and incremental: start with a runbook dry run, then perform component failovers, then full cutover drills. Measurements you must capture include time to provision infrastructure, time to restore data, replication lag during the test, and application-level health after failover. Include rollback procedures and ensure data integrity after failed or partial tests. A common mistake is to only test backups or only test infrastructure provisioning—both must be rehearsed together because restoring data without supporting infrastructure or vice versa fails recovery. Runbooks should list prerequisites, automated scripts, manual steps, and clear success criteria. Automate what you can: provisioning templates, blue-green deployment helpers, DNS update scripts, and monitoring alerts that validate health. After every test, conduct a post-mortem and update runbooks to capture discovered gaps. The ultimate goal is to turn a theoretical RTO/RPO into repeatable measured numbers you can present to stakeholders. Testing and Validating Your DR Plan means regular, incremental tests convert rto/rpo assumptions into verified, repeatable outcomes.. In practical terms, turn assumptions into measured evidence. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Test Often
keyIdea.text: Regular, incremental tests convert RTO/RPO assumptions into verified, repeatable outcomes.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Testing & Validation

Testing and Validating Your DR Plan

Tests prove that your RTO and RPO claims are real and repeatable.

Test cadence & steps
  1. Dry run of runbooks and automation.
  2. Component failover (DB replica promotion, instance scaling).
  3. Full cutover drill to recovery region with simulated traffic.
  4. Post-test rollback and post-mortem.
What to measure
Provision time for infrastructure.
Time to restore or promote data to usable state.
Application health and performance after failover.
Replication lag observed during test.

screens.title: Design a DR Strategy for a Multi-Tier App
screens.subtitle: Apply what you've learned to a concrete scenario

narration.text: Now apply the chapter knowledge to a three-tier application scenario where the database requires RPO of five minutes and RTO of thirty minutes, while web and app servers have RPO of one hour and RTO of two hours. The exercise is to choose a DR strategy per tier and list specific AWS services for the recovery region. For the database tier, warm standby is a strong candidate: maintain a near-synchronous replica in the DR region using a managed replication feature, keep a small active replica instance, and automate promotion steps. For web and application tiers, pilot light or automated backup/restore with pre-baked AMIs can be sufficient: keep AMIs and configuration templates in the DR region and use automation to spin up scaled groups. When you document choices, explain how each service helps meet the RTO and RPO and include a short test plan. A frequent learner error is choosing the same strategy for all tiers—optimize per tier to balance cost and recovery. After completing the template, validate your design by describing the restore sequence and the measurable tests you'd run to prove targets are met.

keyIdea.title: Activity
keyIdea.text: Choose per-tier strategies, list services, and create a short test plan to prove RTO/RPO targets.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Design Activity

Design a DR Strategy for a Multi-Tier App

Use the template below to document tiered choices for the given RTO/RPO requirements.

Scenario
Three-tier app in us-east-1.
Tier 1 (Database): RPO 5 minutes, RTO 30 minutes.
Tier 2 (Web/App): RPO 1 hour, RTO 2 hours.
Template (fill in)
**DR Strategy Design for Multi-Tier Application**

**Application Tier: Database (Tier 1)**
* **RPO:** 5 minutes
* **RTO:** 30 minutes
* **Chosen DR Strategy:** Warm Standby
* **AWS Services & Implementation:**
  1. RDS cross-region replica - continuous replication and fast promotion.
  2. Smaller DB instance in us-west-2 kept active + automated promotion scripts.
  3. Infrastructure-as-code templates for VPC and security groups to speed provisioning.

**Application Tier: Web/Application Servers (Tier 2)**
* **RPO:** 1 hour
* **RTO:** 2 hours
* **Chosen DR Strategy:** Pilot Light (or Backup & Restore with automation)
* **AWS Services & Implementation:**
  1. AMIs in us-west-2 and S3 for static assets - quick instance launches.
  2. Pre-built autoscaling templates and CloudFormation templates for faster scaling.
  3. Periodic snapshots and an RDS read replica if needed for session data.
Assessment & Validation
Test plan
Dry run of promotion, scale-up rehearsals, measure time to reach healthy state, and verify data consistency.
Common error
Choosing costly active-active for tiers that do not need it rather than mixing strategies by criticality.
Takeaway
Match each tier to the minimum strategy that meets its RTO/RPO and test the plan end-to-end.

narration.text: These three concept cards summarize the primary DR strategies and definitions you must recall. Backup and Restore trades low ongoing cost for longer recovery times and relies on tested restore procedures. Pilot Light maintains a minimal active core so you can scale up faster than a full restore. Warm Standby is a reduced-capacity active deployment that can be scaled to full capacity quickly. Learn and recite these short definitions so you can explain them concisely to stakeholders. When asked, respond with the recommended strategy by citing both the RTO/RPO it supports and the characteristic cost profile. This verbal shorthand helps stakeholders understand why you recommend a plan and prevents reflexively choosing the most expensive option. Keep these core concepts top of mind as you design and test DR plans. Key Concepts — Part 1 means remember the trade-off: lower rto/rpo requires more cost and operational effort.. In practical terms, essential definitions and strategies. A simple real-world example is helpful here, because students learn best when they can connect the idea to a familiar situation. This matters because it gives the learner a clear mental model and helps them connect the concept to later examples and problems. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Summary
keyIdea.text: Remember the trade-off: lower RTO/RPO requires more cost and operational effort.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts — Part 1

Core strategy summaries for quick recall.

Backup and Restore
Restore data to new infrastructure in a recovery region. Low cost, higher RTO/RPO.
Pilot Light
Keep a minimal core running and replicate data so scale-up is faster than full restore.
Warm Standby
A scaled-down but functional deployment that can be scaled to handle production load quickly.
Bottom Line

Select the least costly strategy that meets per-tier RTO and RPO and validate it with tests.

narration.text: These final cards capture two technical definitions and a practical reminder that will guide implementation and testing. Multi-Site Active/Active offers the fastest recovery with near-zero data loss but requires duplicate running capacity and careful consistency design. RTO is the maximum acceptable downtime and RPO is the acceptable data loss window; both must be declared by stakeholders before a strategy is chosen. The reminder: always test. Unvalidated plans are liabilities. Use these short concepts when documenting architecture decisions, scoping tests, and communicating trade-offs to non-technical stakeholders. A clear, simple narrative tied to the business cost and tolerance numbers will make your DR recommendation defensible and actionable. keyIdea.text: Drive decisions with stakeholder RTO/RPO, cost, and test results—not with default assumptions.

content.html:
Module 07 › Chapter 7.4 › Key Concepts

Key Concepts — Part 2

Definitions and practical reminders for implementation.

Multi-Site Active/Active
Full active deployments in multiple regions for immediate failover and minimal data loss.
RTO
Recovery Time Objective — the maximum acceptable downtime after an incident.
RPO
Recovery Point Objective — the maximum acceptable age of recovered data, i.e., data loss tolerance.
Remember

Test DR plans often and report measured RTO/RPO values to stakeholders along with cost and operational assumptions.

ai_generation_note: Create a 10-minute animated explainer video comparing the four DR strategies. Use a visual timeline to clearly show the RTO and RPO differences for each. For each strategy, use a simple diagram to illustrate the architecture (e.g., a primary region with a database, and a secondary region showing only backups for Backup and Restore, then a small database for Pilot Light, scaled-down servers for Warm Standby, and full active servers for Multi-Site). Include a section discussing the cost vs. RTO/RPO trade-offs. The interactive element should be a drag-and-drop exercise to match scenarios with the correct DR strategy.
